newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries lower in London, focus on Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries lower in London, focus on Greenspan.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries dipped in London on Tuesday but were expected to remain rangebound over the next few days with little economic data to sway the market and paper from two- and five-year auctions to be absorbed, analysts said.
Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to the senate budget committee hearing on the state of the U.S. economy at 1500 GMT will provide the main market focus for this session, they said.
"Treasuries prices are mostly weaker since Friday's (New York) close, a stronger dollar notwithstanding," said Charles Quigley, U.S. bond salesman at Chase in London.
"Overall it is relatively light on the data front and unless Greenspan says something significant, supply will be the main issue for the next few days."
The 30-year benchmark bond was at 95-19 by 1037 GMT, yielding 6.848 percent, compared with 95-28 at the Tokyo close. The U.S. market was closed on Monday for a holiday.
At the short end of the curve, two-year notes were trading at 99-17 to yield 6.007 percent, slightly lower than 99-18 at the Tokyo close.
Quigley said there was some European buying early in the session, possibly prompted by the strength of the dollar and the weaker than expected Ifo index from Germany.
"That gave Treasuries a minor fillip, but since then they have subsided," he said. "Possibly people are profit-taking ahead of Greenspan's testimony and also over supply concerns."
The U.S. Treasury is due to auction $17.5 billion of two year notes on Wednesday and $12.5 billion five-year notes on Thursday.
David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International in London, also said Treasuries were lower ahead of Greenspan's testimony.

"The basic view before the opening was that we're due for a bit of a bounce, the market has been sagging a little bit," he said. "The fact that hasn't happened shows the market is still cautious ahead of Greenspan."
He said a possible move on U.S. interest rates in February would make it difficult for the market to trade higher. The next Federal Open Market Committee meeting is on February 4 and 5.
Hewitt said the yield curve had steepened considerably over the past month.
"The mood is still very defensive across the curve. I think people will maybe move shorter," he said.
Quigley said the lack of fundamental data suggested Treauries would be rangebound, for now.
"In the short run I would be a better buyer on dips, but it should be a fairly two-sided market in that respect," he said.
March T-bond futures were also lower at 110-17 in automated trade, compared with 110-30 at the January 17 settlement.
